Article Title: How Gujarat's villagers turned mangroves into a natural coastal shield
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In the 1980s, when much of Gujarat’s coastline was losing its mangrove cover, some coastal communities began protecting the few patches that remained. What looked like a small act of conservation would eventually become part of one of India’s most striking mangrove recoveries.Government data shows just how dramatic that transformation has been.According to the Forest Survey of India (FSI), Gujarat had around 427 sq km of mangrove cover in 1987. By 1999, that figure had more than doubled to 1,031 sq km. It reached 1,164.06 sq km in 2023, making Gujarat home to nearly one-quarter of India's mangrove cover. In 2026, the cover has grown to 1177.27 sq km.It attributes the growth to a combination of large-scale plantation programmes, public-private partnerships, community participation and better protection of existing forests.Mangroves are much more than trees growing in salty mud.Their dense network of roots holds sediment together, reduces coastal erosion and slows waves and storm surges before they can reach settlements further inland. The forests also provide breeding and nursery grounds for fish, crabs and other marine species, making them important to both coastal ecosystems and livelihoods.The numbers also reveal how significant Gujarat's recovery has become.The state's 1,164 sq km of mangroves in 2023 accounted for 23.66% of India's entire mangrove cover, second only to West Bengal.But the recovery has not been a simple story of trees being planted by the government. In several parts of Gujarat, conservation efforts have involved coastal communities in protecting and regenerating mangrove areas. That local involvement matters because mangroves occupy a difficult landscape — one constantly shaped by tides, salinity, grazing, cutting and human activity.The government has now taken the approach nationwide through MISHTI, launched in 2023 to restore and promote mangrove ecosystems along India's coast. Under the programme, mangroves are increasingly being treated as natural infrastructure — ecosystems that can perform some of the protective functions that would otherwise require expensive coastal engineering.Gujarat's story therefore offers an unusual lesson in climate protection: sometimes the most effective coastal defence is not something built against the sea.It is something that grows between the land and the sea.And in Gujarat, decades after villagers began protecting those seemingly insignificant patches of mangrove, they have grown into forests spanning more than 1,100 sq km — forming a vast, living barrier along one of India's most exposed coastlines.
Article Summary: Gujarat's 1,164 sq km of mangroves in 2023 accounted for 23.66% of India's entire mangrove cover, second only to West Bengal. Government attributes growth to plantation programmes, public-private partnerships, community participation and better protection of existing forests.

The discussions covered bilateral ties, trade, investment, defence, energy, technology, connectivity, critical minerals and major regional and global developments.The engagements took place as India hosted the Brics Summit under its 2026 chairship, with the expanded grouping bringing together countries with differing geopolitical positions. The bilateral meetings provided New Delhi an opportunity to advance its own strategic and economic priorities alongside the broader summit agenda.Also check: 'Thank you for making New Delhi Summit a success'- PM Modi's Brics 2026 closing address On September 11, PM Modi held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.The Modi-Putin meeting focused on the India-Russia strategic partnership, with the two leaders reviewing cooperation across defence, energy, trade, infrastructure, technology, critical minerals and civil nuclear energy.They also discussed the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the West Asia situation and their impact on maritime trade and the safety of Indian seafarers.PM Modi reiterated India's position that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward for resolving conflicts. The two sides also discussed efforts to increase bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030.PM Modi also met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, with the discussions covering India-Iran relations, Brics cooperation and developments in West Asia. PM Modi reiterated India's support for dialogue and diplomacy and stressed the importance of lasting peace and stability in the region.On the same day, PM Modi met UN Secretary-General António Guterres, adding a multilateral dimension to his diplomatic engagements.On September 12, PM Modi held bilateral meetings with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Vietnamese leadership and Chinese President Xi Jinping.The meeting with Xi was among the most closely watched engagements of the summit. The two leaders discussed the India-China relationship, the boundary question, peace and tranquillity along the border, economic and trade ties, supply chains and people-to-people exchanges.PM Modi stressed that differences should not become disputes and underlined the importance of mutual respect, sensitivity and interest in guiding bilateral relations.The meeting with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim covered areas including trade, investment, defence, semiconductors, infrastructure, the digital economy, energy and fintech.PM Modi's meeting with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation and India's engagement with Africa.He also held talks with UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with discussions centred on the India-UAE strategic partnership and cooperation in areas including defence, technology, energy, critical minerals and connectivity.On September 13, PM Modi held bilateral meetings with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye.He also held engagements with the leadership of Uganda and Nigeria, according to the schedule of bilateral meetings.The meetings broadened India's diplomatic outreach across Africa, Central Asia and Southeast Asia, with discussions focused on strengthening bilateral partnerships and expanding cooperation in areas of mutual interest.The engagement with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa was particularly relevant to the Brics grouping, as South Africa is one of the founding members of the expanded bloc and an important partner for India in advancing the interests of the Global South.The meetings with Egypt and Burundi further strengthened India's engagement with African partners, while the talks with Kazakhstan expanded India's outreach in Central Asia.The Philippines engagement added another important Southeast Asian dimension to PM Modi's diplomatic schedule, alongside his earlier meeting with Malaysia.The 15 formal sit-down meetings were accompanied by several shorter pull-aside interactions with other visiting leaders and representatives of international institutions.The diplomatic activity underlined the importance India attached to bilateral engagement during its Brics chairship. While the summit provided a platform for collective discussions among the expanded grouping, the sidelines allowed PM Modi to address country-specific priorities directly with individual leaders.The meetings also came at a time of heightened geopolitical uncertainty, with conflicts in West Asia and Ukraine affecting energy markets, maritime trade and global supply chains.For New Delhi, the three-day diplomatic marathon offered an opportunity to simultaneously deepen strategic partnerships with Russia and the Gulf, stabilise ties with China, maintain engagement with Iran and strengthen India's outreach to Africa, Central Asia and Southeast Asia.The 15 sit-down bilaterals, combined with the additional pull-aside meetings, therefore formed a significant part of PM Modi's diplomatic outreach during India's 2026 Brics chairship.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi held 15 sit-down bilateral meetings with heads of state and government over three days on the sidelines of the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi. The discussions covered bilateral ties, trade, investment, defence, energy, technology, connectivity, critical minerals and major regional and global developments.

Article Title: 'World expects concrete results': PM Modi extends best wishes as Brics chairship passes to China
Article Text:
China will assume the rotating Brics presidency in 2027 and host the 19th Brics Summit.

PM highlights Global South’s growing trust

Xi calls for stronger Brics role

China proposes five initiatives

PM Modi shares summit photographs

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday extended his best wishes to China, which will host the next Brics summit in 2027, saying the world now expects “concrete results” as the grouping entered its third decade.Addressing the open session on the second and final day of the Brics Summit in New Delhi, PM Modi said, “Brics is poised to enter its third decade. The world now expects concrete results from us, not just ideas and commitments. I am confident that through our collective efforts, we will certainly live up to these expectations.”The Prime Minister also thanked the leaders and their teams for making the New Delhi Summit a success and wished China well as the next host of the grouping.“I extend my best wishes once again to China as the next host of Brics. I especially commend all of you and your teams for making the New Delhi Summit a success. I wish you all a pleasant and safe journey,” he said, according to ANI.Speaking at a session on “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth,” PM Modi said the trust of Global South nations in Brics had grown.He highlighted the grouping’s initiatives on disaster management, cooperation among micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), and environmental protection.“India has advanced the spirit of friendship, partnership, and cooperation through the Brics platform,” PM Modi said.“We have endeavoured to ensure that Brics cooperation is not limited to governments alone; we want our entrepreneurs, farmers, researchers, women, youth, and ordinary citizens to become active participants as well,” he added.“I can say from personal experience that the trust of Global South nations in Brics has grown, because their voices are heard, their experiences are respected, and solutions are crafted not just for them, but with them. The strength of Brics lies in our diversity and cooperation. We may be rooted in different realities, but together we rise through cooperation and blossom for humanity. May our diversity remain our identity, our cooperation serve as our inspiration, and our progress benefit all of humanity,” he noted.Chinese President Xi Jinping called for a stronger role for Brics in advancing the interests of the Global South, urging the grouping to “seize the historical initiative” and become an “active, stabilising and positive force in international affairs”.Addressing the second session of the 18th Brics Summit, Xi thanked PM Modi and the Indian government for hosting the two-day summit.According to an official statement released by China’s ministry of foreign affairs, Xi said the Global South had emerged as a “key driver of world multipolarity” and urged Brics countries to work together to advance its interests.“To bring stability to the world and make it a better place, Brics countries must seize the historical initiative, rally the Global South, be an active, stabilizing and positive force in international affairs, and advance the well-being of all humanity,” Xi said.Xi called for greater participation of developing countries in global decision-making and stressed the importance of multilateralism.“All countries, regardless of their size, strength or wealth, are equal members of the international community,” he said, urging Global South countries to “hold high the banner of multilateralism” and uphold the authority and role of the United Nations.He also backed reforms to the international financial architecture to increase the “representation and voice of developing countries”. Xi called for greater cooperation through the New Development Bank.On development, Xi said Global South countries should remain committed to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. “To achieve great things, one should always put the people first,” he added.Xi outlined five initiatives to deepen Brics cooperation in artificial intelligence, trade and investment, digital industries, intelligent manufacturing, and science and technology talent development.Under the AI initiative, China proposed establishing a Brics AI open-source community, supporting cooperation in developing and applying large language models, and organising specialised AI seminars and training courses.“First, the open source and inclusive AI initiative. China will be a pioneer in establishing a Brics AI open source community, support cooperation in developing and applying large language models, hold specialized AI seminars and training courses, and build an open ecosystem for AI,” Xi said.On trade and investment, China proposed a Brics special economic zone partnership and announced plans to hold the Brics Forum on Trade in Services next year.“Second, the trade and investment facilitation initiative. China proposes to establish a Brics special economic zone partnership, under which countries can set up an intelligent portal, coordinate policies, and build a new frontier for open development. In an effort to cultivate new drivers of economic and trade cooperation, China will hold the Brics Forum on Trade in Services next year. We welcome your active participation,” he added.China also proposed a Brics digital ecosystem cloud platform and cooperation in digital skills, technology exchange and industrial development.“Third, the digital industry cooperation initiative. China will push for establishing a Brics digital ecosystem cloud platform, and conduct digital skills training, technological exchange and industrial alignment, so as to jointly enable the development of the digital economy,” Xi said.Under the intelligent manufacturing initiative, China offered to assist fellow Brics countries in building smart factories and developing common standards.“Fourth, the intelligent manufacturing cooperation initiative. China stands ready to assist fellow Brics countries in building smart factories and developing standards and norms, and jointly promote manufacturing transformation and upgrading,” he said.Xi also proposed a Brics engineer cultivation alliance and a youth exchange programme for scientific and technological innovation.“Fifth, the science and technology talent development initiative. China proposes to set up a Brics engineer cultivation alliance for joint development of engineers and mutual recognition of competency standards. China will launch a Brics youth exchange program for scientific and technological innovation, so as to cultivate more high-caliber talent,” he said.Xi called for a people-centred approach to emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, and backed the creation of a global AI governance framework based on consensus.He also urged stronger cooperation on climate change and called for the “full and effective implementation of the Paris Agreement”.As India concluded its 2026 Brics chairship, Xi said China would continue to promote high-quality development, high-standard opening up and cooperation with other countries. Xi later departed New Delhi after attending the two-day summit.PM Modi also shared a series of posts and photographs from the summit on X. “Brics Summit related interactions continue at Bharat Mandapam,” he said in one post, sharing photographs with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.He also posted a photograph of Brics leaders at the summit’s family photo event.“With leaders of Brics Member and Partner Countries, Outreach Invitees and Heads of International Organisations together at Brics Summit in New Delhi. A powerful reflection of the growing strength and global resonance of the Brics family. We are connected by a shared vision of cooperation, furthering the spirit of partnership and progress,” he wrote.Earlier, PM Modi welcomed the leaders of Brics member and partner countries, outreach invitees and heads of international organisations at Bharat Mandapam.“Another productive morning at Bharat Mandapam. Happy to welcome the Leaders of Brics Member and Partner Countries, Outreach Invitees and Heads of International Organisations,” he said in another post. China will assume the rotating Brics presidency in 2027 and host the 19th Brics Summit.
Article Summary: PM Modi extends his best wishes to China, which will host the next Brics summit in 2027. PM Modi said the world now expects “concrete results” as the grouping entered its third decade. Chinese President Xi Jinping called for a stronger role for Brics in advancing the interests of the Global South.

Article Title: Beyond 'seek help': What happens when students reach out for mental health support?
Article Text:
How well do India’s systems support students in crisis? (File Photo)

How serious is India’s student suicide crisis becoming?

Student suicides in India rose by 4.3 per cent in 2024.

Are India’s institutions failing students in crisis?

Concerning findings from the 2026 National Task Force (NTF) report on student mental health in India.

If help exists, why are students still afraid to use it?

What happens after a student calls for help?

How should students and systems respond?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Imagine finally admitting that you need help and dialling a 24/7 national mental health helpline, hoping a person will answer, only to hear: “All our counsellors are busy attending to other callers. This is taking more time than expected.” On some calls we made to TELE MANAS at 14416, the wait crossed 10 minutes, and choosing the callback option produced no return call. For a student who may already have spent hours deciding whether to reach out, those minutes arrive after the difficult part has supposedly been done.Versions of this moment have followed India through 2026, as student suicides have continued to surface from IIT campuses to coaching hubs such as Kota. World Suicide Prevention Day, earlier this week, returned with the theme “Changing the Narrative on Suicide”, once again urging people in distress to speak and seek support. The appeal raises another question that receives far less attention: once someone does speak, what awaits them?“Serious lapses” and “gross negligence” were the words a University Grants Commission (UGC) committee used while examining how Fakir Mohan Autonomous College in Odisha handled complaints from a 20-year-old B.Ed student. She had complained of alleged sexual harassment by her department head before dying after setting herself on fire on campus in July 2025. The committee also described the response to her complaints as marked by “insensitivity”.At KIIT in Bhubaneswar, 20-year-old Nepali student Prakriti Lamsal had reported harassment before she was found dead in her hostel in February 2025. A UGC committee later said the university failed to lawfully act on her complaints and concluded that the tragedy “could have been averted”.In Dharamshala, the father of a 19-year-old student had warned her college that she was being “bullied and ragged” and was in “utter depression”; after her death, a UGC inquiry found that “no one contacted the student or her family”.“A suicidal thought is a signal of significant psychological distress, not something that should be dismissed or moralised,” says clinical psychologist Apoorva Krishnan, co-founder of Oorvai Wellness. “What matters is understanding the immediacy and severity of the risk.” The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), which compiles India’s official suicide statistics, recorded another rise in student suicides in 2024, continuing a decade-long increase, although those figures cannot reveal whether a student had complained or sought help before their death.What happens when an institution has already identified a student as vulnerable, yet the hostel warden responsible for their everyday residential life remains unaware? The Supreme Court-appointed National Task Force (NTF), created to address student mental-health concerns and prevent suicides, encountered precisely such a situation during one of its field visits. The student had already been identified as vulnerable, but that information had not reached the hostel warden.The NTF reviewed 31 centrally funded institutes, including 23 IITs and four IIMs, of which only 18 reported at least one mental-health service provider. At some institutes, faculty mentors or peer counsellors were counted alongside trained mental-health professionals, meaning that the people included under the broad category of “support” could have very different responsibilities and levels of expertise. For a student facing serious psychological distress, those differences determine who can recognise the level of risk and what happens after it is recognised.“The most important thing is that an institution should have a clear response pathway before a crisis happens,” Krishnan says. “We cannot expect an individual teacher or counsellor to figure out what to do in the moment.” The concern becomes especially immediate when an institution has already identified a vulnerable student but the people closest to their everyday environment remain outside that information loop.“They’ve been told; they’ve been conditioned to think that they can manage everything on their own. So, I think it’s an internal conflict that they have to first fight in order to come to us,” says a Delhi University counsellor, on the condition of anonymity.Once a student decides to seek help, the burden should shift to the institution. Yet only 43 per cent of students surveyed by the NTF said they knew their institution facilitated counselling. If support exists but students do not know where to find it, how accessible is it really?Capacity creates another fault line. “We are only two psychologists in college and there are about 7,000 students,” the counsellor says. “Even if each one of us is able to take in 15 to 20 clients, we are only able to cater to 40 students in a week. There are still a lot of students who want to take sessions and we would not be able to cater to them.”The strain continues behind the counselling door. “We get paid very little as compared to the work we do,” she says. “There’s also lack of supervision. We pay for our own supervision and if we’re taking supervision from good, seasoned psychologists, the fees is huge.”For a system that asks counsellors to hold students through moments of serious distress, that support cannot depend only on personal commitment. “Sigmund Freud says that psychoanalysis is a cure through love, and I’m a firm believer of this that this job of taking care of other people’s minds requires us to carry that love.” The question for institutions is whether that care is being properly staffed, supported and sustained.A successful call can still mark the beginning of another journey if the counsellor decides that the person needs care beyond the conversation and refers them to another professional or a hospital. The crucial question then becomes whether the caller reaches that next point of care and whether anybody knows if they do not. For someone already experiencing severe distress, each additional appointment or journey becomes another step they must manage.Tele-MANAS had handled 43.64 lakh calls by August 11, 2026 through 53 cells covering every state and Union territory in 20 languages. By March, 47,487 callers had been referred for non-emergency in-person care, while more than 5,000 urgent referrals had been made to psychiatric hospital emergency departments. Government data does not show how many of those callers subsequently received the recommended care or how quickly that care reached them.“Follow-up is not optional,” Krishnan says, because making a referral does not establish whether the person in crisis actually reached the hospital or professional to whom they were directed. A caller may have completed one difficult act by asking for help and then find themselves responsible for navigating the next stage alone. The effectiveness of the referral therefore depends on what happens after the number is handed over.“The immediate priority is safety, not solving the person’s entire life,” Krishnan says, explaining that someone who may act on suicidal thoughts should move somewhere safer and avoid being alone. Asking a trusted person for company can begin with a sentence as simple as: “I am not feeling safe being alone right now. Can you stay with me?” If an attempt has already occurred or the situation is life-threatening, emergency medical help becomes necessary.Even putting distress into words can feel overwhelming, which is why Krishnan says, “Help-seeking doesn’t begin by having a detailed conversation or even being verbal.” A student can send a message or show somebody something they have written when speaking feels too difficult. They can simply say: “I don’t know how to explain this, but I need help.”What happens after those words are heard cannot rest entirely with one professional, particularly when the student will eventually return to the academic and residential environment in which their distress developed. “The counsellor cannot be the institution’s entire suicide-prevention system,” Krishnan says. “If the student returns to the same academic, interpersonal or residential environment without any coordination or support, we have not really addressed the problem. ”The student at the beginning of this story has already picked up the phone, while another student may have entered a counselling room or told somebody that they no longer feel safe. In each case, the act that every awareness campaign asks for has already happened because the student has reached out. What follows is the question Krishnan leaves with the system: “What happens next, who is responsible for it, and how do we know that the student has actually received help?”
Article Summary: Student suicides in India rose by 4.3 per cent in 2024. If help exists, why are students still afraid to use it? What happens after a student calls for help? How should students and systems respond? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Article Title: NHRC in collab with MEA to organise on capacity building programme on human rights for functionaries of Global South

NEW DELHI: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) in collaboration with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), is organising a six-day Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) executive capacity building programme on human rights for senior-level functionaries of National Human Rights Institutions (NHRIs) of the Global South. It will be held from Sept 14 to 19 in Delhi.The programme will be inaugurated by the Chairperson of NHRC, India Justice V. Ramasubramanian. “The programme aims to strengthen the capacities of participating NHRIs and facilitate the exchange of experiences and good practices, with a view to promoting cooperation in the advancement and protection of human rights in their respective countries,” the Commission said in a statement.The customised programme has been developed based on the needs of participating NHRIs and the feedback received during the four previous ITEC capacity-building programmes organised by the Commission. Forty-one senior-level functionaries from 15 NHRIs are expected to attend.The NHRC said that the programme will cover themes including the development of international human rights framework, contemporary human rights issues, human rights and business, impact of new technology on human rights and sustainable development.Participants will also gain insights into NHRC, India’s functioning, including its complaint management and investigation mechanisms, in the context of global human rights discourse.Drawing on NHRC, India’s experience of over three decades, the programme seeks to promote mutual learning and meaningful collaboration among NHRIs for advocacy, enforcement and institutional strengthening across the Global South.Eminent persons with domain expertise in capacity building and training will serve as resource persons.Participants will engage in interactive sessions with leading practitioners, cultural immersion and field visits. The programme will provide opportunities for dialogue and exchange among NHRIs of the Global South, reflecting NHRC, India’s commitment to strengthening human rights institutions and cooperation across the region.
Article Summary: NHRC and MEA to hold six-day ITEC capacity building programme on human rights for 41 functionaries from 15 Global South NHRIs from Sept 14. The programme will be inaugurated by the Chairperson of NHRC, India Justice V. Ramasubramanian.

Article Title: Japan nuclear operator chief to quit after quake data scandal, reactor restart plans hit
Article Text:
The Hamaoka plant is located in Omaezaki close to the expected route of a major Pacific earthquake.

Data scandal puts restart plans at risk

Japan seeks to revive nuclear power

The president of Chubu Electric Power is set to step down after a scandal involving manipulated earthquake data at its Hamaoka nuclear plant, Japanese media reported on Monday. The company is also expected to abandon plans to restart two reactors at the facility.President Kingo Hayashi and chairman Satoru Katsuno will resign, according to public broadcaster NHK and other local media. Chubu Electric is expected to hold a press conference later on Monday. The company was not immediately available for comment.The Hamaoka plant is in central Japan, near a seismic fault line and an area considered vulnerable to a major earthquake. It has been undergoing regulatory safety checks as Chubu Electric seeks approval to restart two reactors.In January, the operator admitted that it had submitted data to regulators that underestimated the earthquake risks facing the plant. The Nuclear Regulation Authority suspended its safety review process for Hamaoka in late December.A 250-page report by an independent panel, released on Monday, said management pressure contributed to the misconduct. It said the management’s "reprimand" over delays in the restart review had placed pressure on employees and was "one of the factors contributing to the misconduct".The Nikkei business daily reported that Chubu Electric would withdraw its application for the safety review.The estimate of maximum seismic ground motion is a key factor in designing nuclear plants to withstand earthquakes. In September 2023, the NRA approved Chubu Electric’s estimate of 1,200 gal, a unit used to measure ground acceleration during an earthquake.However, the regulator received information from a whistleblower in February last year about possible data fraud.The Hamaoka plant is located in Omaezaki, in Shizuoka prefecture, close to the expected route of a major Pacific earthquake. In 2024, the Japan Meteorological Agency issued its first special advisory over the possibility of a "megaquake" in the Nankai Trough area. The advisory was lifted a week later.Japan largely abandoned nuclear power after the 2011 earthquake and tsunami caused reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi plant to melt down. The country is now seeking to restart nuclear facilities to reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels, meet rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence and achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.The world’s largest nuclear power plant, Kashiwazaki-Kariwa, resumed operations earlier this year.
Article Summary: President Kingo Hayashi and chairman Satoru Katsuno will resign, according to public broadcaster NHK and other local media. Chubu Electric is expected to hold a press conference later on Monday. The Hamaoka plant is in central Japan, near a seismic fault line and an area considered vulnerable to a major earthquake.

Article Title: Gujarat to global: How idea to fix pollution has lessons for Delhi
Article Text:
For Delhi-NCR, which is annually in the news for its winter air pollution crisis, the Gujarat experience also offers a useful model

Indian solution goes global

TOI

.





NEW DELHI: Nearly 15 years ago, a handful of economists, engineers and regulators began wrestling with a question in Gujarat. Could factories be persuaded to cut pollution without fearing a shutdown?Today, that experiment has an answer in the emissions trading scheme (ETS), which is travelling nearly 14,000 km from India, poised to become one of the country’s newest environmental exports.After transforming industrial pollution regulations in Gujarat and inspiring similar programmes in Maharashtra and Rajasthan, the idea that germinated in India is headed to Rio de Janeiro.The Brazilian city has signed a letter of intent to examine adapting this approach to its own pollution challenges.If implemented, Rio would become South America’s first emissions trading system for industrial partic­ulate pollution.For Delhi-NCR, which is annually in the news for its winter air pollution crisis, the Gujarat experience also offers a useful model, which is centred around incentives that make industries compete to pollute less, rather than punishing them when they pollute more.For decades, India’s industrial pollution control has relied largely on periodic inspections and shutdown notices when factories breached emission limits.Researchers believed there was a better way — one that rewarded environmentally cleaner factories, instead of treating every factory in the same way.The idea is simple. Regulators set a maximum pollution limit for an industrial cluster and divide it into permits.Factories that cut emissions beyond their target can sell surplus permits to plants finding it harder or costlier to clean up. Cleaner factories can earn, while others get flexibility to comply. At the same time, the pollution stays within the overall cap.The approach was piloted in Surat in 2019 by researchers affiliated with the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) and J-PAL, which was working with Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB).The pilot covered 162 of Gujarat’s 317 large coal-burning industrial plants, while the rest remained under conventional regulation, allowing researchers to compare the two approaches.In the randomised trial, the participating plants cut particulate emissions by 20-30% and pollution-control costs by 11%. Compliance touched 99%, against roughly two-thirds under the conventional system.Researchers estimated the benefits exceeded costs by at least 25 times.Conventionally, a typical plant emitted around 1,300 kg of particulate matter a month.Emissions from similar industries operating under the ETS fell to roughly 900-1,000 kg a month — a 20-30% reduction that held across all 10 compliance periods during the nearly two-year study from April 2019 to 2021.The flexibility built into the system allowed firms to meet their pollution commitments more efficiently and at a lower cost. “This pollution market was made in India, tested in India and it succeeded in India.Just as pollution doesn’t respect borders, ideas don’t respect borders too,” said Emissions Market Accelerator (EMA) co-chair Michael Greenstone, one of the four researchers who worked with GPCB on the experiment.For Dr Kaushik Deb, the executive director of EMA, the challenge lay in convincing industrial units that cleaner air need not come at the expense of growth.“The first reaction was, ‘why another form of regulation?’ But we created the scheme such that there were no losers,” Deb toldOnly one industrial closure occurred under the system in seven years, he said.Today, the programme covers a population of nearly 300 million across the country and is expanding to sulphur dioxide and wastew-ater pollution.Dr Bala Srinivasan, the EMA co-chair, said the international journey accelerated after Gujarat became an Earthshot Prize Finalist in 2025. Founded by Prince William, the prize identifies and helps scale breakthrough environmental solutions from thousands of entries worldwide.“Earthshot suddenly gave us a lot of global exposure,” Srinivasan said. That visibility, he said, helped open conversations beyond India — including Rio — and generated fresh interest among Indian states as the prize prepares to come to Mumbai later this year.For Delhi-NCR, the Gujarat experiment offers a different way of thinking about industrial pollution, and gives industries an economic reason to reduce emissions, rather than relying only on inspections, penalties and shutdowns.While the pollution problem of the national capital region is far more complex than Surat’s industrial cluster, and the Gujarat model cannot simply be transplanted, the experts suggest that less emission across sectors can become a competitive advantage rather than merely a regulatory burden.In a region where repeated restrictions have often produced friction between pollution control and economic activity, that may be a lesson worth examining.
Article Summary: Rio de Janeiro has signed a letter of intent to examine adapting this approach to its own pollution challenges. If implemented, Rio would become South America’s first emissions trading system for industrial partic­ulate pollution. For Delhi-NCR, the Gujarat experience also offers a useful model.

Article Title: Residents of Charholi battle lack of access roads, water & power woes
Article Text:
With traffic flowing only through one road, chaos ensues as congestion becomes a norm

Issues at a glance





PUNE: For more than 10,000 residents living across eight housing societies in Charholi’s Pride World City township, stepping out of their neighbourhood each day feels less like a commute and more like an ordeal.Nestled amid rapidly developing localities like Lohegaon, Dhanori, Wagholi and Kharadi, Charholi was marketed as Pune’s next residential hotspot.But behind the towering apartment complexes and promises of worldclass connectivity lies a very different reality: A township effectively dependent on a single lifeline road to Pune city limits, plagued by chronic traffic snarls, water shortages and erratic power supply. Residents say they are living in a neighbourhood that has grown faster than the infrastructure meant to support it.“We have just one access road to get to PMC limits, which for us is crucial as most of us work in companies in Kharadi, Magarpatta and Viman nagar. Access to the airport is also via this single road,” IT profession al Dhananjay Ashok Deshmukh said.“It passes through a narrow private road provided by Ajeen kya DY Patil University and then merges onto the already choked Porwal Road.If that private road is closed even for a day, more than 10,000 people would be as good as isolated. Other roads exist only on paper. On the ground, they are dead ends,” he said.Charholi's rapid growth was fuelled by ambitious promises of connectivity through the proposed outer and inner ring roads, and a 90mwide arterial road that was supposed to link to Wagholi and Spine Road.Years later, plans re main confined to blueprints while residents continue to navigate pot holed roads and gridlocked traffic. During school hours, the situation descends into complete chaos.“In mornings and after noons, when school buses enter the stretch, traffic comes to a standstill. If a PMPML bus and a school bus arrive from opposite directions, the road locks up entirely. Parents are anxious about letting children travel alone. On top of that, poor roads have led to multiple accidents, with bikers frequently skidding on damaged stretches,” resident Kshitija Tilekar said.Despite repeated attempts to engage with Pimpri Chinchwad Municipal Corporation (PCMC), resi dents claim they have largely been met with silence.“We don’t want another temporary fix,” IT professional Vinay Tatti said. “There are several roads that can be opened and integrated into a proper traffic plan. Some smaller internal roads could even function as oneway corridors to ease congestion. A parallel road to Porwal Road was acquired nearly three months ago, but no work has started. It remains inaccessible,” he said.For many, the consequences go far beyond inconvenience. Pune airport, located barely 7km away should be reachable within 1520 minutes. Instead, residents often spend more than an hour on narrow and congested approach roads.“Even ambulances struggle to reach us because of the traffic,” said resident Virendra Gambhir, who has lived here since 2018. Gambhir recalls experiencing this firsthand after suffering a serious fall in Dec 2020.“A hospital just 5km away took me nearly three hours to reach,” he said, add ing, “I was fortunate that someone offered me a ride because getting an auto or cab is almost impossible here. Even after being discharged, every followup visit became exhausting and stressful because of traffic and terrible roads.”According to Gambhir, complaints filed through PCMC’s Sarathi app and emails sent to officials between Dec 2020 and April 2022 yielded little result.“My online complaints were routinely closed without any resolution, and my emails went unan swered,” he said. Water Tank Next Door, But No Flow in Taps Roads are only one part of the crisis.Residents point to an over head water tank standing right beside the township as a symbol of the area’s infrastructure paradox. Despite its presence, households remain heavily dependent on tanker water supplied by the developer at subsidised rates. “We spend nearly Rs1 crore every year on tanker water,” said resident Dhruv Malhotra.“There is an overhead reservoir next to us, but the infrastructure required to bring water into our homes simply doesn’t exist. We are paying water tax as part of our property tax and then paying again for tankers.” Power Problems Add To Residents’ Misery If traffic and water shortages were not enough, residents say unstable electricity supply has become yet another daily struggle.“So many appliances have been damaged because of voltage fluctuations,” said Tilekar. “Almost every day, someone reports a short circuit or a damaged appliance.”Residents point out that the issue has already been acknowledged at the highest levels. In July 2023, chief minister Devendra Fadnavis reportedly raised the need for additional land allocation for an MSEDCL substation to strengthen power infrastructure in Charholi.While the proposal was subsequently approved, locals say there is little evidence of work starting on the ground. For a locality marketed as Pune’s future growth corridor, residents say the future continues to remain frustratingly out of reach.Until the promised roads, water infrastructure and power upgrades materialise, many in Charholi feel they are living in a township that is expanding rapidly but remains disconnected from the city around it.Civic Body Blames Terrain For Water Supply Woes Vijay Singh Bhosale, executive engineer of PCMC’s water supply department, said the township was facing water supply issues because it was located on elevated terrain.“The area is uphill, making it difficult to pump water to the storage tank near the township. We have already laid a pipeline and are planning to build another tank at a lower level to collect water and then pump it to the exist ing tank for distribution to the societies. However, this depends on receiving additional water from Bhama Askhed. At present, there is no alternative solution. The issue will be resolved once we are able to lift more water from Bhama Askhed,” Bhosale said.TOI also contacted the builder to understand coordination undertaken with civic authorities. Arvind Jain, managing director of Pride Group, said the company had been consistently engaging with the corporation to address residents’ concerns.“Connectivity within PCMC limits is largely adequate, but the airport link has remained stalled for years. A land acquisition issue involving a missing road link has now been resolved through efforts by our legal team and the corporation’s legal team. I have also invested funds to help move the project forward. Once the land is acquired, the road can be con structed, easing connectivity issues. Traffic congestion towards Vimannagar persists because of narrow roads, but the corporation is working on widening them. Development work on Porwal Road, Bharat Mata Road and Dhanori Road is also under way, and at least two of these stretches should see improvement by the end of the year,” Jain said.On water supply, Jain said necessary infrastructure was in place and PCMC was providing water, though the quantity might be insufficient.“There is no infra related water issue, but there are financial challenges associated with procuring tanker water. To support residents, we are providing tankers to societies at subsidised rates.We remain in constant touch with civic authorities to help resolve issues and minimise inconvenience to residents,” he added
Article Summary: More than 10,000 residents live in Charholi’s Pride World City township. The township is effectively dependent on a single lifeline road to Pune city limits. Residents say they are living in a neighbourhood that has grown faster than the infrastructure meant to support it.

Article Title: Businessman paid Rs 6.42 lakh for foreign business travel using wife’s card and then reimbursed her; taxman disallowed it, ITAT Mumbai says nothing in law bars it
Article Text:
The individual said he reimbursed his wife after returning to India. (Image for representative purpose only)

What the case is about

Income mismatch between books and Form 26AS

Business expenses paid using his wife's credit card Difference between the income reported in Form 26AS and the man’s books of account

How did the man win the case in ITAT Mumbai?

What ITAT said

You incur business expenses on your wife’s credit card and reimburse her. But the tax department raises an objection. This is what happened with a Mumbai-based business man, who then won partial relief from the ITAT.The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ruled that genuine business travel expenses do not become disallowable merely because they were initially paid using his wife’s credit card and later reimbursed to her.The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) Mumbai has provided partial relief to a businessman after the income tax department disallowed Rs 6.42 lakh of his travel expenses because the payments had been made using his wife's credit card.In its judgment, Challa Nagendra Prasad, Judicial Member, and GM Doss, Accountant Member, held that there is no legal bar on a person using their spouse's credit card to meet business expenses and subsequently reimbursing the spouse for those payments.The ruling arose from a tax dispute involving a resident of Mumbai. According to the submissions before the tribunal, the man traveled to Paris, Russia and other destinations for business purposes and incurred total travel expenses of Rs 20.32 lakh.Of this amount, Rs 6.42 lakh was paid through his wife's credit card. The individual said he reimbursed his wife after returning to India.The arrangement, however, came under scrutiny during assessment. The Income Tax Department treated the Rs 6.42 lakh as unexplained, arguing that the man’s wife had no connection with his business travel and that the expenditure had been incurred through her credit card. The Assessing Officer (AO) consequently disallowed the Rs 6.42 lakh from the man’s business expenditure.The AO also questioned another portion of the businessman’s travel expenses. Since Rs 1.49 lakh had been paid in cash, the officer disallowed 20% of this expenditure on the ground that the expenses could not be completely verified.A further 20% disallowance was made on the remaining foreign travel expenses of Rs 12.4 lakh. The AO said the man had not furnished adequate details of the foreign travel, including information about the people who travelled and the services they provided.The assessment also raised a separate issue concerning the income reported by the taxpayer.According to the AO, Form 26AS showed the man’s income at Rs 79.87 lakh, whereas his books of account reflected income of Rs 75.51 lakh. The difference worked out to Rs 4,36,400, which the AO sought to bring to tax.The dispute before the tax authorities therefore involved two separate issues:The individual first challenged the assessment before the Commissioner of Appeals (CIT A), but his appeal was rejected.He then approached ITAT Mumbai. On August 31, 2026, the tribunal granted him partial relief on the disallowance relating to travel expenses paid through his wife's credit card, according to an ET report.However, it did not finally decide the issue concerning the Rs 4,36,400 difference between Form 26AS and the books of account. Instead, the tribunal sent that matter back to the Assessing Officer for verification.Pranshu Goel, Partner at Ashok Pranshu & Co., told ET, that ITAT Mumbai ruled in the man’s favour after finding that the disputed expenses were genuinely incurred for foreign business travel. The fact that the payments were initially made through his wife's credit card and later reimbursed to her did not change the nature of the expenditure.The tribunal held that there is no provision under the law preventing a taxpayer from using his wife's credit card to meet business expenses. Pranshu said the tribunal also rejected the argument that the reimbursement represented payment for services provided by the man’s wife and therefore required tax deduction at source, since she had not rendered any independent service.Using a family member's credit card for personal or other expenses can be a common practice, particularly to earn reward points, cashback or travel benefits, Pranshu said. However, he cautioned taxpayers against overlooking the documentation.Pranshu advises: "However, taxpayers must preserve the complete documentary trail, purpose, invoices, card statements and proof of reimbursement to substantiate that the expense is for the purpose of business and is not a personal expenditure."He also pointed out that high-value credit card transactions are now reported and reflected in AIS/TIS. As a result, spending that appears disproportionate to the cardholder's disclosed income could attract scrutiny from the tax department unless the source of the payment and subsequent reimbursement are properly explained.During the proceedings, the individual’s chartered accountant provided details of the foreign business travel. He told the tribunal that the man had incurred Rs 3.97 lakh for travel to Metal Expo in Russia and Rs 4.94 lakh for travel to CNR Expo in Istanbul, Turkey.Together, these expenses amounted to Rs 8.91 lakh. The CA said a portion of this expenditure had been paid through the man’s wife's credit card. To support the claim, he submitted the expenditure details along with his wife's bank account statement.The CA also cited a previous ITAT Mumbai ruling in the case of Girish Raghavan, ITA No. 6955/Mum/2025, dated March 4, 2026.The tribunal accepted the argument that using a spouse's credit card to incur business expenses was not prohibited by law.“There is nothing in law which precludes an assessee from incurring business expenditure through the credit card of his spouse and thereafter reimbursing the said expenditure to the spouse.”ITAT Mumbai further found nothing improper in such an arrangement for meeting business expenses.The finding also went against the reasoning adopted by the CIT (A). The appellate authority had held that the man should have deducted TDS on the reimbursement to his wife if the transaction was being treated as payment for services she had independently provided.The tribunal rejected that interpretation, observing:“No payment was made towards any service rendered by Smt. Shah; the amount was merely reimbursed to her since her credit card had been utilised for incurring the expenditure. The addition on this count is, therefore, unwarranted and is directed to be deleted.”Relying on the Girish Raghavan precedent cited by the CA, the tribunal also deleted the ad hoc disallowances relating to the travel expenditure.The separate discrepancy between the income reported in Form 26AS and the books of account was not finally decided by ITAT Mumbai. Instead, the tribunal sent the matter back to the Assessing Officer to examine the reconciliation statement submitted by the man and pass a fresh order in accordance with law after giving the assessee an adequate opportunity of being heard.
Article Summary: Mumbai-based business man won partial relief from the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. Tribunal ruled that genuine business travel expenses do not become disallowable merely because they were initially paid using his wife’s credit card. Tax dispute arose from a tax dispute involving a resident of Mumbai.

Article Title: Africa world's most active terrorism theatre; reports more than two-thirds of ISIS activity: Report
Article Text:
Africa has emerged as the world's most active terrorism theatre, according to a new US House Homeland Security Committee report.

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the top priority in preventing modern terrorist threats? Strengthening intelligence Monitoring online platforms International cooperation Preventing radicalisation 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Africa has emerged as the world's most active theatre of terrorism, with more than two-thirds of Islamic State (ISIS) activity taking place on the continent, according to a new report by the US House Committee on Homeland Security.The report, released in lieu of the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks, said seven of the 10 countries with the highest number of terrorism-related deaths were in Africa, with five concentrated in the Sahel.It warned that the geographic shift in jihadist activity was creating new challenges for US counterterrorism efforts, with intelligence coverage and resources remaining uneven across the continent.The report, titled “25th Anniversary Report: National Security Improvements and the Domestic Threat Landscape 25 Years After 9/11/01,” assesses how the US security landscape has changed since the attacks and identifies emerging threats facing the country.“While terrorism has shifted geographically, it has also evolved operationally,” the committee said, pointing to the growing role of decentralised attacks and individuals radicalised without formal links to terrorist organisations.According to the report, more than two-thirds of ISIS's global activity during the first half of 2025 occurred in Africa, citing data from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project. It also cited the Global Terrorism Index, which found that ISIS and its affiliates were responsible for 1,805 deaths across 22 countries.The committee said the concentration of jihadist violence in Africa had exposed intelligence gaps and strained global counterterrorism resources.The shift is particularly significant because US counterterrorism policy has historically focused heavily on the Middle East, while the African theatre presents different challenges, including fragile governments, limited intelligence collection and uneven information-sharing capabilities.The report warned that extremist networks operating in Africa were increasingly using migration routes, smuggling networks and online platforms to extend their influence beyond the continent.The committee also said the nature of terrorism itself had changed since 9/11.Rather than relying exclusively on hierarchical organisations such as al-Qaida, extremist movements increasingly seek to inspire individuals to carry out attacks independently.The report said ISIS had encouraged supporters to launch attacks wherever they lived, reducing the need for direct command and control.It pointed to the January 2025 ISIS-inspired attack in New Orleans and the arrest of two US citizens the following month over an alleged ISIS-inspired plot in Michigan as examples of the changing threat.The number of radicalised young people with no formal affiliation to extremist organisations has also increased by more than 300% over the past decade, according to the report.Online propaganda, encrypted communications and social media have helped accelerate radicalisation while reducing the need for formal terrorist networks.The committee said this required a shift from an “organisation-centric” approach to counterterrorism towards prevention based on individual behaviour.The report also said the definition of the terrorist threat had widened considerably.The US has expanded its Foreign Terrorist Organisation framework to include violent cartels and other transnational criminal organisations, while also designating ideologically diverse extremist groups.The committee said this reflected a broader change in which terrorism, organised crime and foreign influence increasingly overlap.It cited Iran as an example of a state actor using criminal and terrorist proxies in overseas operations.The committee also warned that terrorism was increasingly intersecting with cyber capabilities.Terrorist organisations, criminal networks and hostile states are exploiting encrypted platforms, social media and emerging technologies including artificial intelligence, drones and 3D-printed weapons, it said.AI could help defenders analyse large amounts of security data and identify suspicious activity, but the same technology could also allow malicious actors to conduct reconnaissance, social engineering and vulnerability research faster and at greater scale.The report said the next phase of terrorism would be shaped as much by digital platforms and algorithms as by physical safe havens and battlefields.
Article Summary: Seven of the 10 countries with the highest number of terrorism-related deaths were in Africa, with five concentrated in the Sahel. More than two-thirds of ISIS's global activity during the first half of 2025 occurred in Africa. The shift is particularly significant because US counterterrorism policy has historically focused heavily on the Middle East.

Article Title: One of Meta's 'most famous' AI researchers, who left the startup he co-founded to join Meta, is quitting in less than a year; had reportedly waited to...
Article Text:
Andrew Tulloch, who reportedly turned down Meta's $1.5 billion offer before joining, is now leaving for Anthropic

Andrew Tulloch waited for Meta's Muse AI agent to launch before quitting

Meta's reported $1.5 billion offer made Tulloch the face of the AI talent war

Tulloch helped train OpenAI's GPT-4o, GPT-4.5 and o3 models

Anthropic lands Tulloch as AI labs keep trading top researchers

Andrew Tulloch, the AI researcher Meta once chased with a pay package reportedly worth up to $1.5 billion, is leaving the company after less than a year. He is joining Anthropic, the maker of Claude. The Wall Street Journal reported the move, and an Anthropic spokesperson later confirmed to Business Insider that Tulloch starts next week on its inference and performance team. He will work on how the company's AI models are trained and how they respond to users.Meta loses one of its highest-profile hires. Tulloch rejoined the company in October 2025 after leaving Thinking Machines Lab, the startup he co-founded with former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati. He worked in TBD Lab, the small team central to Mark Zuckerberg 's AI strategy, within Meta Superintelligence Labs led by Alexandr Wang. His personal website described his role as "working on superintelligence."Tulloch told colleagues he was leaving on Wednesday, a day after Meta launched Muse. He had reportedly held off on quitting until the product shipped. Muse is a personal AI agent built for mainstream users rather than developers. If given access, it can send emails, shop online and complete other tasks on a user's behalf.Why he is leaving remains unclear. Meta declined to comment on his exit, according to The Wall Street Journal, and Tulloch did not respond to requests for comment.Tulloch's name became tied to the AI hiring frenzy last year. According to The Wall Street Journal, Zuckerberg first tried to buy Thinking Machines. When Murati refused, he approached more than a dozen of her employees, with Tulloch as his main target. The package could have been worth up to $1.5 billion over at least six years, assuming top bonuses and exceptional stock performance.Tulloch said no. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone called the reported figure "inaccurate and ridiculous." Months later, Tulloch joined Meta anyway. The terms he finally accepted were never disclosed.Tulloch spent 11 years at Facebook and rose to distinguished engineer, one of its highest technical ranks. In 2023, he moved to OpenAI, where he helped train GPT-4o, GPT-4.5 and o3, before co-founding Thinking Machines in early 2025.OpenAI had tried to hire him years earlier. In 2016, OpenAI president Greg Brockman wrote to Elon Musk that Tulloch earned $800,000 a year at Facebook, while OpenAI offered recruits a $175,000 salary plus a $125,000 bonus, per the Journal. Tulloch balked at the pay cut.Tulloch is the third Thinking Machines co-founder to change jobs in recent weeks. Barret Zoph and Luke Metz, who had moved from the startup to OpenAI, left last month for Google and Meta respectively. Google's chief scientist Jeff Dean also quit last month with three senior researchers to launch an AI startup.For Anthropic, the hire comes at a busy time. Business Insider reported that the company is preparing for its initial public offering. This week, it also lost researcher Jacob Coxon, who resigned with a public warning that people building AI believe it could wipe out humanity by the end of the decade.Meta spent last year showing it would pay extraordinary sums for AI talent. Eleven months after Tulloch finally said yes, its most famous recruit is heading to a rival.
Article Summary: Andrew Tulloch, who reportedly turned down Meta's $1.5 billion offer before joining, is now leaving for Anthropic. He will work on how the company's AI models are trained and how they respond to users. He is the third Thinking Machines co-founder to change jobs in recent weeks.

Article Title: ARC raises Rs 10.5 crore in pre-seed funding
Article Text: ARC, a gaming technology company has raised Rs 10.5 crore in pre‑seed funding led by Chimera VC and MIXI Global Investments, with participation from Dhruv Vohra, Director, Meta, APAC, in his personal capacity. The funding will accelerate development and commercialisation of ARC X1, covering hardware engineering, product validation, manufacturing readiness, and further development of OWL OS and ARC’s gaming software platform. It will also support team expansion, go‑to‑market capabilities, and strategic partnerships across gaming, cloud, content and technology.The global portable gaming console market was valued at US$3.89 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow at 9.7% CAGR through 2033. ARC aims to tap into India’s large mobile‑first gaming community and the low penetration of dedicated gaming hardware, creating space for a more accessible portable gaming category.Founded by Jobin Joseph and Kaustubh K. Jadhav, ARC is building a platform that integrates hardware, software and gaming experiences. The ARC X1 is a portable gaming system designed to make dedicated gaming more accessible to Indian gamers.ARC is developing its own hardware and software stack, aiming to build an ecosystem across devices, operating systems, software services and gaming experiences.Joseph said the funding will deepen ARC’s technology, accelerate product development and move the company closer to launch. Jadhav added that ARC was founded on the belief that access should not determine how deeply someone experiences gaming, and the funding will help bring ARC X1 to gamers at scale.Chimera VC’s Krish Anurag said ARC fits their thesis of backing companies that can become infrastructure for the next chapter of gaming. MIXI Global Investments’ Tomoharu Urabe said ARC X1 can make handheld gaming more accessible for India’s passionate gaming community.ARC X1 is built on ARM architecture, powered by Qualcomm technology, and runs OWL OS, ARC’s proprietary gaming operating system. It supports native Android gaming, PC‑game compatibility through ARC’s software stack, and cloud gaming. ARC has crossed 50,000 waitlist sign‑ups and collaborated with Qualcomm ahead of launch, adopting a community‑led development model involving gamers through early testing and feedback programmes.
Article Summary: ARC is building a platform that integrates hardware, software and gaming experiences. The ARC X1 is a portable gaming system designed to make dedicated gaming more accessible to Indian gamers. ARC has crossed 50,000 waitlist sign‑ups and collaborated with Qualcomm ahead of launch.
